sections.h2: What the Recorder does when a house sells
sections.html:
The Recorder logs the deed that moves title to the buyer, along with mortgage releases and liens tied to the house, so the public can find them later. In Coconino County that work happens in Flagstaff. The county's online records portal puts the Treasurer, Assessor, GIS and Recorder links on one screen, which is handy when you are checking several things at once.

The counter is at 110 East Cherry Avenue, first floor, in Flagstaff, and it is staffed weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Call before you go.

Plenty of sellers never see the counter. A title or escrow company drafts the deed, collects signatures, pays the charge and files it. Still, if you know what the office requires, you can spot mistakes early, especially on family or inherited transfers where people often prepare papers themselves.

Arizona sets recorder charges in A.R.S. 11-475, and the standard price is $30 for each instrument. Copy and certificate fees come from the same statute.

ServiceFee
Standard recording of a deed or similar paper$30 per instrument
Recording requested by a federal, state or local government party$15 per instrument
Copy, prepared and certified$1 per page or partial page
Recorder's seal and certificate on a copy$3 more
Certificate under section 47-9523$10 per name, plus $1 for each financing statement or assignment listed

Both the $30 and the $15 already include a charge collected under section 11-475.01. A state agency pays half price for copies it needs for official use. Restitution liens and liens to enforce support orders are recorded and released at no charge, and no fee is collected where public money would be paying another county office.

Have escrow itemize every recording charge on your settlement statement. The Coconino County line should read $30 per instrument, or more when several papers are filed at once, like a deed and the release of an old lien. The full text of the statute is at azleg.gov for anyone who wants the exact wording.

Under A.R.S. 11-1133, a deed that passes title, or a contract for sale of real property, generally carries a sworn affidavit of legal value. Buyer and seller sign it, or an agent signs for either. The form is the Arizona Department of Revenue's. An incomplete affidavit with no exemption noted on the paper means the recorder must refuse it.

Gather these details before the signing, since the form wants every one of them:

  • Contact information for buyer and seller: names, mailing addresses and phone numbers.
  • An address for future tax statements.
  • Legal description, street address and sale date.
  • Total price, any cash down payment, and how the purchase is financed: cash, a new third-party loan, a seller loan, an assumption, or an exchange.
  • Whether personal property worth five percent or more of the price is part of the deal.
  • The assessor's parcel number.
  • Any relationship between the parties and other conditions of the sale.
  • Use of the property. For a house, say whether it will be owner-occupied or rented.

Answer every line or write not applicable. Leaving one blank is a frequent reason a package is sent back.

sections.h2: Do gift deeds and family transfers need the affidavit?
sections.html: Not always. Section 11-1134 names the transfers that are exempt, and a deed of gift is one of them. Write the exemption on the face of the deed. A wrong claim can hold up your recording, so talk it through with the Recorder or your title company before you sign.

sections.h2: Format rules that get a document rejected
sections.html:
Section 11-480 of the state code limits when a recorder may refuse a paper at the counter, and the list is short. The instrument needs a caption naming what it is, for example warranty deed. It has to be an original, signed in original ink, legible enough to copy, no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, with type no smaller than ten point.

Leave two inches blank at the top of page one for the recording stamp, and keep every other margin at half an inch or more. A first page that misses the top margin can be fixed with a cover sheet carrying the title. If your paper amends one already on record, it must cite the earlier recording date and its docket and page.

Once the recorder accepts the paper, a later claim that it broke these rules does not invalidate it.

sections.h2: Get the tax balance before you record
sections.html:
The Coconino County Treasurer is at 110 E. Cherry Avenue in Flagstaff, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. Reach the office at (928) 679-8188, toll free at (877) 500-1818, or at treasurer@coconino.az.gov.

The year's tax attaches to the house as a lien on January 1, which is why you want the balance before the deed goes on record. Escrow typically pays the Treasurer from your proceeds at closing, and the deed is submitted to the Recorder afterward.

sections.h2: If you are selling from out of town
sections.html:
Escrow or title staff usually submit the recording and pay the fee for you. If you plan to handle a family or estate transfer yourself, call the Recorder first and ask which forms the office wants. A recorded instrument needs original signatures, so a photocopy of a signed deed will not work. Mail the original, or arrange for a signing near where you live and send the signed paper to the office.

A short checklist keeps the process moving:

  1. Confirm the legal description and parcel number against your tax bill.
  2. Sign the deed in front of a notary, in ink.
  3. Complete the affidavit of legal value or note the exemption.
  4. Pay the Treasurer's balance through escrow.
  5. Record the deed, then keep the recording information with your closing papers.

Selling for cash removes the lender from the picture. There is no buyer's mortgage to wait for, so fewer papers need to be matched and recorded, and the deed of trust that would normally follow your deed never appears. You still need the same core items: a deed with original signatures, an affidavit of legal value or exemption, a tax payoff from the Treasurer, and the recording fee. Ask escrow to walk you through each item and the date it is due, so there are no surprises on closing day.

Flagstaff is both seat and largest city of Coconino County, which spans 18,661 square miles. In 2020 the census found 145,101 people and 69,108 housing units, of which 25.7 percent were vacant and 59.2 percent of occupied units were owner-occupied. Reservation land covers 7,142 square miles, so a parcel near it deserves an early question to your title company. A Flagstaff bungalow, a Page rental and a Williams cabin all follow the same state recording steps.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Coconino County?
faqs.a: The state charge is $30 per instrument for most papers, and the county applies the same flat fee to ordinary recordings. A government party asking for the recording pays $15 per instrument.

faqs.q: What is an affidavit of legal value?
faqs.a: It is a form that buyer and seller, or their agents, sign to report the price, financing, parcel number and other sale details. The recorder must reject a deed lacking it unless the deed cites an exemption.

faqs.q: Does a deed of gift need the affidavit?
faqs.a: No. A.R.S. 11-1134 exempts a deed of gift, but the deed must state the exemption on its face. Check with the Recorder or a title company first.

faqs.q: How big can a recorded page be, and what margins does it need?
faqs.a: No larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, with type of at least ten point, a two inch top margin on page one and half inch margins elsewhere. A cover sheet can rescue a first page that comes up short.

faqs.q: Where is the Recorder's counter in Coconino County?
faqs.a: It is at 110 East Cherry Avenue, first floor, in Flagstaff, open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Call ahead before you visit.
